briefOverview: This chapter links Israel’s worsening oppression in Egypt with a theological claim that God is guiding events toward Israel’s later recognition of him. It also narrates a separate international conflict in which Zepho of Chittim defeats an African coalition after appealing to the God of the patriarchs.
summary:
Levi dies in Egypt at 137 years old, and after the patriarchal generation passes, Egyptians increasingly oppress the Israelites, confiscating their property and subjecting them to harsh labor.

A new Pharaoh (Melol) rises after a regime change, and a generation that “had not known” Joseph and his brothers comes to power; the text portrays Israel’s affliction as ultimately “from the Lord” for Israel’s future good, so they might know God, witness signs and wonders, fear God, and walk in his ways.

Separately, Angeas king of Africa raids toward Chittim, but Zepho (son of Eliphaz, grandson of Esau) destroys his troops, prompting Angeas and his brother Lucus to muster a massive army to retaliate.

Zepho seeks military help from Edom but is refused due to an old peace covenant; the people of Chittim then urge Zepho to pray to the God of his ancestors, and Zepho petitions the God of Abraham and Isaac, repudiating the nations’ gods as “vain.”

God hears Zepho “on account of Abraham and Isaac,” and Zepho wins two major battles, inflicting enormous losses; Angeas’s forced conscription still fails, and Angeas and Lucus flee back to Africa in fear of Zepho thereafter.
externalContext:
The Book of Jasher is a later Jewish work of “rewritten Bible” that retells and expands stories known from the Torah, often adding genealogical details and extra narrative episodes not found in the canonical text. Its surviving forms were transmitted in medieval Jewish tradition and later printed; it is not generally treated as part of the biblical canon in Judaism or most Christian traditions.

The chapter’s depiction of a new Egyptian leadership that no longer recognizes Joseph echoes a common ancient Near Eastern theme: political memory and patronage can disappear rapidly when dynasties change, especially when a favored minority loses its former protector.
externalReferences:
The oppression of Israel after the death of Joseph’s generation closely parallels Exodus 1:6–14, including the rise of a new king and the escalation of hard labor.

The claim that Israel’s suffering serves a later good—so that they might know God and witness his mighty acts—fits the broader Exodus pattern where God’s “signs and wonders” in Egypt lead to recognition and reverence (e.g., Exodus 7:3–5; 10:1–2).

Zepho’s appeal to the God of Abraham and Isaac and the emphasis on covenantal remembrance echoes the recurring biblical motif of God acting “for the fathers’ sake” (cf. Exodus 2:24; 6:5).
practicalQuestions: When circumstances worsen after supportive leaders are gone, how can a community maintain identity and hope without relying on lost protections?
What does it look like to interpret hardship as potentially formative without minimizing injustice or excusing oppressors?
Zepho rejects “the gods of the nations” as ineffective; what modern substitutes for trust in God function like “vain” gods in practice (security, status, power)?
How can prayer grounded in remembered commitments (covenant, promises, core values) shape courage and decision-making in a crisis?
uncertainAreas: The identities and locations of “Chittim,” “Africa,” and the figures Angeas/Lucus/Sosiphtar are not clarified within the chapter, and it is uncertain how (or whether) these names map onto known historical peoples or places rather than serving as legendary or literary-geographic markers. The chapter also implies long time spans (Melol’s 94-year reign; Israel’s 102nd year in Egypt) without synchronizing them to any externally verifiable chronology.
